title: How Jay-Z’s Yankee Stadium Shows Came Together: As Told by Young Guru, Omar Edwards & Adam Blackstone
summary: Three of Jay's closest collaborators provide an inside look at the road to his Yankee Stadium trifecta.
contentText:
“Just to think that it’s been 30 years, and now a younger generation gets to see what legacy looks like,” Young Guru says of Jay-Z’s Yankee Stadium three-peat. Two weeks later, the impact of Hov’s Bronx trifecta is starting to cure. 

Jay has delivered plenty of memorable performances throughout his Hall of Fame career: Carnegie Hall featuring a 40-piece orchestra, the 10th anniversary of Reasonable Doubt at Radio City, his Fade to Black “farewell” at Madison Square Garden, and opening Brooklyn’s Barclays Center in 2012, to name a few. 

When Jigga announced the first two anniversary shows celebrating 30 years of Reasonable Doubt and 25 years of The Blueprint in March, there was an added layer of anticipation for Hov’s return atop the rap pantheon, while breathing life into a genre with a dearth of superstars rising to prominence in the 2020s.

At 56, could this be the last time we see Jay take the Yankee Stadium stage and pull off a star-studded show of this magnitude? That thought seemed to play a role in the chaos that led to Sunday’s Extra Innings madness, which saw unticketed fans rush the gates and cause a multi-hour delay.

Billboard spoke to three of Jay’s closest collaborators: Young Guru , who met Hov in the late ’90s and has served as his engineer and DJ for over two decades, longtime bassist Adam Blackstone and Jay’s music director Omar Edwards for an inside look at how the Yankee Stadium mini-residency came together. 

Act I:

Edwards and Jay-Z began ideating in March while exchanging plans for the Yankee Stadium shows, but their focus largely remained on Jay’s return to the stage in Philly as a headliner at Roots Picnic in May. When the calendar flipped to June, all eyes shifted to Yankee Stadium — or as Jay told GQ when it comes to his motto for 2026, “all offense.” 

That text thread between Hov and Edwards quickly expanded to include Blackstone, Guru and Khirye Tyler (Beyoncé’s music director). Edwards estimates there were “30-40 edits” of back-and-forth, with Jay before finally nailing the structure of the shows.

During this time, Blackstone was locking down an all-star 10-piece band, forming an 18-piece string section and recruiting a horn arrangement that can learn three very different shows in a matter of weeks.

“All of this is Jay’s vision; we make suggestions. Jay gives a yes or no on things that he likes, and he comes with suggestions of what he would like to see,” Guru says. “But once Jay makes a final decision, it’s our job to go execute that.”

One of those suggestions came from The Roots’ Questlove, who proposed to have night two to celebrate all three installments of The Blueprint series. But Jay adapted the idea to focus on the much-beloved first installment, which turns 25 this September.

Rehearsals began on June 18 and took place in New York, giving Jay and the entire team three weeks to perfect the show before the curtain dropped. The plan was to dedicate a week to each of the shows, but that didn’t end up happening. 

Young Guru points to the tedious process of figuring out the key of every song in the setlist, as well as drops to properly tie the narrative of the show together. Even having to chart all of the music for the horns and string section to read added another layer of challenges when planning.

“This was just extremely difficult, because it’s three different shows back to back to back, where we wouldn’t get another week of rehearsal before the next show,” Guru adds.

By this point, Edwards was coordinating with various teams contributing to the show, whether that be with Jay’s creative director Willo Perron, or with Gabriel Moses and Renell Medrano, who helmed the visuals projecting to the upper deck.

July 10 crept up in a blink. It was a serene 75-degree night at Yankee Stadium, oozing with hype that outweighed even the World Series games hosted in The Bronx two years prior. Three decades after releasing his first LP, Jay took his victory lap at Yankee Stadium with a love letter to his fans, celebrating his years-in-the-making debut, which has long outlived its commercial performance at the time of its release (No. 23 peak on the Billboard 200 ).

Jay once described RD as the “realest album” of all-time , as he narrated his street tales and evolution as a Brooklyn hustler from Marcy Houses with dexterous raps. “Friday night had a very retrospective fan moment where… it wasn’t quiet, but it was very intentional,” Blackstone reflects. “[Fans] listening to the words, I felt people remembering where they were when he was given this game.”

The first surprise of the night came when Jay brought Beyoncé out to fill in for Mary J. Blige on “Can’t Knock the Hustle,” and then a hard stop was built into the setlist following “Politics as Usual.” That got Adam Blackstone’s antennas up that Jay had a few things to get off his chest with a freestyle, since a similar stop in the setlist was used in May at Roots Picnic .

“The transition called for a hard stop. So once that was built in, I was like, ‘Uh oh, here we go,’” he recalls. Jay responded to the backlash for his business deal with Target, and then seemed to allege that former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick — who never played in another game following the 2016 season where he took a knee during the national anthem for social injustice — reached a financial agreement with the NFL to remain silent on the matter going forward.

“Buddy took a check/ I ain’t even mad at him,” Hov rapped. “But along with that check you have to sign a non-disparagement/ I’m the one they can’t control.”

Jay also sparred with The Notorious B.I.G. on the jumbotron for their majestic “Brooklyn’s Finest” collaboration, which featured a refreshed arrangement with different classic Biggie instrumentals. Edwards reveals that “Hypnotize” was originally there in place of the “One More Chance” beat, until Hov made the call to swap them in June.

Nas joining Hov on stage drew the biggest pop of the night from the 45,000 Roc-A-Fella faithful in attendance, with a moment that rap fans couldn’t imagine when the legendary duo were at each other’s throats 25 years ago. That striking visual will live on long after both hip-hop deities hang up their mics for good.

Plenty of other special guests also hit the stage, including Jay’s daughter, Blue Ivy, who played the piano to “Feelin’ It,” as well as ’00s collaborators Alicia Keys and Memphis Bleek. But it was Jaz-O who provided Guru’s favorite moment of night one, when he joined Hov for “Bring It On,” and Jay gave his mentor his flowers.

“If you’re going to give anybody credit for me being on this stage tonight, give it to that man Jaz-O, right there,” Jay saluted Jaz. A fellow Marcy Houses native, Jaz-O gave Jay an example of someone who could make it out through rap, and provided Hov with opportunities to sharpen his pen and follow in his footsteps. The two had a falling out in the early 2000, but eventually made their way back.

“That just touched my heart,” Guru admits. “I love that part of it, and it’s very meaningful for people that have been following Jay from the beginning.”

Just when fans thought the show was over, Keys showed up, with Hov then delivering an encore that was completely improvised. Guru jumped around Jay’s discography with a mix of hits and deep cuts, hopping from The Dynasty ’s “Change the Game” to “Do It Again,” as the duo leaned on over two decades of chemistry.

“That part is unplanned. You never know when he’s gonna do that,” Guru explains. “I just have to stay ready as someone who’s been with him for so long. I never know if he’s gonna just walk off stage — or I’ve even gone to him at times and said, ‘He…
